definition: A vital breath or energy that animates living things and moves through the cosmos. In Daoist thought, cultivating qi is part of health, ritual and immortality.
Complementary forces of dark and light, cool and warm, rest and motion. They are not simply good and evil, but paired qualities that balance and transform into one another.
The Way: the underlying order or process of the cosmos. Daoist texts describe it as something that cannot be fully named or grasped by ordinary language.
An immortal or transcendent being. Xian are often imagined living in remote mountains or floating among the clouds, having escaped ordinary death through cultivation, elixirs or divine favour.
The Chinese dragon, a powerful water creature associated with rain, rivers, storms and good fortune. Unlike many European dragons, it is often benevolent and linked to cosmic order.
A ruler of a sea, lake or river, usually called Longwang in Chinese. Dragon kings control rain and tides, live in underwater palaces, and can be generous or dangerous to humans.
The idea that heaven is organised like an imperial government, with a Jade Emperor, ministries, registers and divine officials. It shapes how many Chinese gods and underworld powers are imagined.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas, a composite text describing strange lands, creatures, gods and rituals. It preserves some of the oldest surviving Chinese mythic material.
A sixteenth-century Chinese novel attributed to Wu Cheng'en, following the monk Tripitaka and his companions on a pilgrimage to India. It is the main source for the Monkey King's adventures.
The idea that a ruler's right to govern depends on virtuous conduct and the welfare of the people. Disasters and rebellion can be read as signs that the mandate has been lost.
